brief.head: Privacy from the state
brief.text: Privacy rules for firms are the eas­ier prob­lem, Ajay Shah said; India has it up­side down. “If there is a need for pro­tec­tion, it is against the state.” {117-C14}

brief.head: Weigh your evidence
brief.text: Weak data that clashes with your prior should move you a lit­tle, Ajay Shah said, and strong data a lot. All mea­sure­ment serves the up­dat­ing of pri­ors. {117-C16}

brief.head: The long tail returns
brief.text: Dialects like Bhojpuri and Haryanvi were swal­lowed by big lan­guages. But mar­kets, Amit Varma said, first ho­mogenise and then em­power in­di­vid­u­als to find the long tail. {117-C10}

brief.head: Lockdown by location
brief.text: Phone lo­ca­tion data showed that the COVID lock­down largely worked, Amit Varma said. Google and Facebook, Ajay Shah added, re­leased mo­bil­ity mea­sures for the whole coun­try. {117-S07}

brief.head: Digital exhaust
brief.text: Emailing, shop­ping, even buy­ing vada pav throws off a trail of data that looks like trash, Ajay Shah said. People are now open­ing that garbage bin. {117-C13}

thought.label: Thought for the day

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on new ways of measuring
lead.head: Read my genes, check my battery

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 117

body: Ajay Shah began with a prin­ci­ple. Knowledge, he said, runs from mea­sure­ment to sta­tis­ti­cal reg­u­lar­i­ties to the­ory: first Kepler, then Newton. “You al­ways start at the data. If you don’t have the data, you don’t have any­thing. Then it’s just con­ver­sa­tion.” {117-C01}

Very lit­tle in India is well mea­sured, he added, and big in­sti­tu­tions such as the Central Statistical Organization and the CMIE were long the only game in town. Over the last twenty years, a rev­o­lu­tion has brought what he called “new eyes” to the world.
Amit Varma had a darker foot­note. “I would say the road to knowl­edge ends in de­spair,” he said, be­fore going on to show what the new data can see.
## Written in our genes

The first kind looks into the past. By 2009, Varma said, full-genome stud­ies of an­cient hu­mans were a full-fledged sci­ence, and they have over­turned much of the re­ceived wis­dom of ar­chae­ol­ogy.

The key find­ing is that we are far more mixed than any­one as­sumed. All of us de­scend from one woman in Africa, known as mi­to­chon­drial Eve. Europe saw five great mi­gra­tions and India four, and many Europeans and Asians carry three to five per cent Neanderthal genes.
“They all get mixed up with each other and we are all fun­da­men­tally one peo­ple,” Varma said. {117-C04}

In India, the genes rule out two po­lit­i­cal myths. There was no clean Aryan in­va­sion, and the Aryans were not the orig­i­nal peo­ple from whom ev­ery­thing came. There was a mi­gra­tion, and then deep mix­ing.
That mix­ing stopped around 100 CE, when a par­tic­u­lar ide­o­log­i­cal strand in the Gangetic belt won out and se­vere caste en­dogamy began. It left a clear sig­na­ture in the genes. {117-S04}
Varma called caste “the deep­est sin of Hinduism, but it’s not the orig­i­nal sin”: the walls are two thou­sand years old, the mix­ing twice that. What was cho­sen, he ar­gued, can be re­versed.
For Shah, the les­son was about method. Careful ar­chae­ol­ogy had left the de­bate to opin­ion; new mea­sure­ment set­tled it. “We brought guns to a knife fight,” he said.
## Phones and satel­lites

The sec­ond kind sits in every pocket. Smart Finance, a Chinese lender, judges bor­row­ers from their phone data, Varma said. If your bat­tery reg­u­larly falls below 12 per cent, you will not get a loan. {117-S06}
Nobody began with a the­ory that a low bat­tery means risk. The al­go­rithm finds the pat­tern across mil­lions of phones and leaves hu­mans to work out why, which also makes it hard to game.

The third looks down from the sky. In 2009, two broth­ers re­mem­bered that Sam Walton, the founder of Walmart, judged a store by the cars in its park­ing lot, and built a firm that counted them by satel­lite. {117-S08}
Shah added oil tanks that be­tray how full they are by the shad­ows in­side them. Varma ended with in­dexes that read the econ­omy from lip­stick, un­der­wear, hem­lines and di­a­pers.
What all of it leaves, Varma said, is a harder ques­tion. “The ques­tion to pon­der on is one of at­tributabil­ity. That if a par­tic­u­lar part of the econ­omy is doing well, why is it doing well?”

second.label: Credit scores
second.head: Rs 80, with interest
second.deck: Amit Varma’s credit card standoff, and why one score can misjudge a person

pic.caption: Amit Varma on his Rs 80 credit card debt

body: About 25 years ago, Amit Varma had a Standard Chartered credit card with no au­to­matic pay­ment. Because he is Bengali, he said, he was lazy, and he waited for the bank to call be­fore pay­ing. Once the amount was so small, Rs 80, that no­body called. {#piddly}

The card was can­celled and his credit score col­lapsed. With in­ter­est, the debt grew to Rs 3,000, then Rs 5,000, and the bank would not send a bill. When it reached Rs 29,000, he re­fused on prin­ci­ple to pay, though he eas­ily could have. {#rs29000}
His score is still bad. Yet he has never had an EMI, and pays ven­dors at once, or in ad­vance. Richer data, he ar­gued, would build a more holis­tic pic­ture. {117-S05}

quote.text: I fancy that if you could see all the other data about me, you would re­al­ize that I’m an ab­so­lutely up­stand­ing cit­i­zen.

third.head: Argentina, priced online

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the Billion Prices Project

body: Roberto Rigobon and Alberto Cavallo thought economies were being mea­sured with a small amount of data when far more was avail­able, Amit Varma said. Their Billion Prices Project gath­ered huge vol­umes of prices from the in­ter­net to build an index of its own.
One find­ing was that on­line prices tracked off­line prices more closely than some had ex­pected, mak­ing them a very good proxy.

The other came from Argentina. Between 2007 and 2015, Varma re­called, the of­fi­cial fig­ure for in­fla­tion was about seven to ten per cent. The scraped data showed 20 to 30 per cent a year. {#argentina}
Eventually, he said, the cri­sis ex­ploded. The les­son he drew: “If you’re build­ing an index, the more di­verse sources you use, the bet­ter it is, the more re­li­able it is.” {117-S12}

box.title: The books behind the genes
box.text: David Reich’s *Who We Are and How We Got Here* ex­plains how full-genome stud­ies over­turned re­ceived wis­dom from ar­chae­ol­ogy. Amit Varma paired it with Tony Joseph’s *Early Indians*, and said he had not stopped think­ing about their find­ings since. {117-R01}

sections.label: The deep past
sections.head: Out of Africa, into the mix
sections.caption: the mixing in our genes
body: Earlier the­o­ries as­sumed that once hu­mans came out of Africa, they set­tled into more or less sep­a­rate pop­u­la­tions, Amit Varma said. Ancient DNA shows we are more mixed up than we thought.

All of us de­scend from one woman in Africa, known as mi­to­chon­drial Eve. Europe has since seen five mas­sive mi­gra­tions. Three to five per cent of the genes of Europeans and many Asians come from Neanderthals, from a time when “we were hav­ing a party with Neanderthals”. {117-J04}
Beneath the vis­i­ble dif­fer­ences, Varma said, there is one in­ter­wo­ven peo­ple. {117-C04}
## Four waves into India

India, as Tony Joseph tells it in *Early Indians*, saw four major mi­gra­tions. The first Indians came out of Africa about 65,000 years ago, and tribal com­mu­ni­ties still carry more of their genes. {#firstindians}

Agricultural peo­ple from Central Asia fol­lowed, bring­ing wheat and bar­ley, and formed the Harappan civil­i­sa­tion. Their lan­guage was prob­a­bly proto-Dravidian, an early ver­sion of Tamil, which is older than Sanskrit. Austroasiatic and Tibeto-Burman peo­ples came into the north-east. About 4,000 years ago came Indo-Europeans from the steppes, with an early form of Sanskrit.

Every Indian car­ries Ancient North Indian and Ancient South Indian genes, in dif­fer­ing de­grees. It was not an in­va­sion, Varma said, but an Aryan mi­gra­tion; and the idea that the Aryans were the orig­i­nal peo­ple is “patent non­sense”. {117-S02}
~ Both David Reich and Joseph, he added, in­sist that none of the re­main­ing dif­fer­ences should be­come a rea­son for racist think­ing.

quote.text: There was an Aryan mi­gra­tion. Right, it wasn’t an in­va­sion, we don’t know that. There was an Aryan mi­gra­tion.

sections.label: The great party
sections.head: The party ended in 100 CE
sections.caption: caste endogamy and the census
body: For about two thou­sand years after the Indo-Europeans ar­rived, Amit Varma said, the genes show full in­ter­min­gling. There was no sense of our peo­ple and not our peo­ple, and no sense of caste.

Then, around 100 CE, a par­tic­u­lar ide­o­log­i­cal strand in the Gangetic belt won out, and se­vere caste en­dogamy began. Upper-caste men also proved more suc­cess­ful at spread­ing their genes than lower-caste men. {117-S04}

Endogamy, Varma ar­gued, meant con­trol­ling fe­male sex­u­al­ity: no af­fairs, no ba­bies with out­siders, no fall­ing in love. Today’s prud­ish moral­ity comes partly from that, and partly from the Victorian moral­ity the British brought. {117-C07}
## Boxes that harden

He also set out a the­ory he sees grains of truth in. The British, whose early in­ter­locu­tors were Brahmin elites, made cat­e­gories of caste and re­li­gion, and being forced to tick one box changed how peo­ple saw them­selves. He called this re­flex­iv­ity, a term he first learned from George Soros.

Ajay Shah saw a state leg­i­bil­ity project with un­in­tended con­se­quences, and a Heisenberg ef­fect: “The state tried to make caste leg­i­ble and in the process it changed the caste sys­tem.” {117-C08}
~ Shah also asked whether smaller jatis fall below a min­i­mum vi­able pop­u­la­tion. If so, he said, the spread of moder­nity would bring a large gain in pub­lic health. {117-C11}

quote.text: if you’re look­ing for a large pop­u­la­tion, look at the Han Chinese, they’re a large pop­u­la­tion. India is many thou­sands of small pop­u­la­tions.
quote.who: David Reich, as recounted by Amit Varma

sections.label: In your pocket
sections.head: Credit where charge is due
sections.caption: the phone as a credit score
body: Our genes are al­ways with us, Amit Varma said, and so are our phones. Smart Finance, a Chinese micro-lender, scores bor­row­ers from their phone data. If your bat­tery reg­u­larly falls below 12 per cent, you will not get a loan. {117-S06}

Filling in your date of birth too fast counts against you, as does mak­ing a typo and going back to fix it. Lenddo, an­other lender, found that a phone al­ways fully charged is also a bad sign. Varma keeps his at about 80 per cent.

A 2018 German study found that Android users de­faulted at about 1.7 per cent and iPhone users at about 1.07. {#iphone} Hotmail and Yahoo ad­dresses, typos in an email ad­dress and ha­bit­ual 2 AM shop­ping also pre­dicted de­fault.
## Nobody knows why

The ma­chine does not start with a the­ory, Varma said. It finds the pat­tern across mil­lions of phones and leaves the why to hu­mans, much as chess play­ers had to re­verse-engineer AlphaZero. A known met­ric can be gamed; thou­sands of un­known ones can­not. {117-C12}
~ Unlike China’s state-run so­cial credit score, which Varma called creepy, this is vol­un­tary: you trade ac­cess to your phone for a loan.

~ After COVID, phone lo­ca­tion data showed the lock­down largely worked. Google and Facebook, Ajay Shah said, re­leased mo­bil­ity mea­sures for the whole coun­try: “a gor­geous pub­lic do­main data re­lease”. {117-S07}

quote.text: If we know met­rics we can game met­rics. But we don’t even know what the met­rics are.

sections.label: Eyes in the sky
sections.head: Watch the ore, not the news
sections.caption: the capsized iron ore train
body: Satellite pic­tures were scarce at first. RS Metrics, Amit Varma said, could get about twelve pic­tures a month, and ex­pen­sive ones. {#twelve} Then the data grew cheap, plen­ti­ful and gran­u­lar, and a field called al­ter­na­tive data was born.
One firm, he said, once claimed to take alt data from a thou­sand ven­dors. It is no longer a niche, bou­tique busi­ness.

A few years ago, a train car­ry­ing some 268 bo­gies of iron ore cap­sized. Stock prices crashed, iron ore prices rose, and the mar­ket ad­justed to the as­sumed loss. But some traders looked at satel­lite im­ages and saw the ore lying flat, easy to reload. {117-S09} They bet on a faster re­cov­ery and made a killing.
## Fair play for the clever

Some call such edges un­fair. Ajay Shah dis­agreed. Finance, he said, gives very smart peo­ple in­cen­tives to pro­duce in­for­ma­tion, and their trad­ing makes prices more ef­fi­cient. “That price is a pub­lic good,” he said, be­cause mar­ket prices run the so­ci­ety.
Speculation is vol­un­tary and meant to be tough, he said. Those who do not feel strong enough should not spec­u­late, and should buy and hold index funds in­stead. {117-C15}
~ Varma made a re­lated point: in time, such data be­comes cheaper and more widely avail­able, and those with­out it should fac­tor that into their de­ci­sions.

quote.text: We should never get into this in­vestor pro­tec­tion when we are dis­cussing spec­u­la­tor pro­tec­tion.

sections.label: The fun chapter
sections.head: Lipstick up, hemlines down
sections.caption: lipstick, underwear and hemlines
body: Amit Varma saved a fun chap­ter for the end, fun, he said, “be­cause I say so”: in­dexes that read the econ­omy from ev­ery­day be­hav­iour.

First, lip­stick. Leonard Lauder of Estée Lauder no­ticed sales ris­ing in the 2001 re­ces­sion. In tough times, he rea­soned, peo­ple stop buy­ing $200 hand­bags but still buy $20 lip­sticks, the cheap­est lux­ury there is. {117-S11}
The pat­tern held in 2008 and 2011, then broke under COVID. “People are wear­ing masks so they don’t need lip­stick,” Varma said. {117-J09}
Alan Greenspan, an econ­o­mist who, Varma said, “loved low in­ter­est rates”, coined the male un­der­wear index: in bad times, men put off buy­ing un­der­wear for as long as they can.
## Hemlines and ba­bies
Hemlines rose in the 1920s and the 1960s and fell in the Depression; after the 1973 oil shock, maxi skirts came into vogue. In 2008, di­a­per sales fell and sales of rash oint­ment rose.

Varma won­dered whether hem­lines track the same na­tional mood as fer­til­ity, which, Ajay Shah had ar­gued, falls in bad or au­thor­i­tar­ian times. Shah cau­tioned that this needs good birth data, the priv­i­lege of rich coun­tries such as South Korea and Japan. {117-C17}
~ The hard part, Varma said, is at­tri­bu­tion: know­ing what is re­ally driv­ing a sig­nal. {117-C18}

quote.text: you want the good life, you want a good so­ci­ety, and then peo­ple will have more chil­dren.

I think dif­fer­ences are amaz­ing. Differences should be cel­e­brated. We are dif­fer­ent in all kinds of di­rec­tions. We are far more alike than we are dif­fer­ent, but the dif­fer­ences are not a prob­lem.

p3.title: Stories from the data
p3.deck: A guitar duo, a scientist’s bet, a curled tongue and a shadowed tank

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on two brothers, a guitar and Walmart’s car parks
stories.head: Count the cars, beat the market
body: In 2009, Tom Diamond went to see his brother Alex, who worked at a firm that sold satel­lite im­agery. A client wanted to buy a fac­tory abroad, and Alex had just used the pic­tures to show that it was rep­re­sent­ing it­self cor­rectly.

The broth­ers had a hobby, Amit Varma said: rock ver­sions of Western clas­si­cal music, and they are known for a ver­sion of one of Schubert’s com­po­si­tions. One day, doo­dling with their in­stru­ments, they won­dered what else the data might be good for.

One of them re­mem­bered Sam Walton. The founder of Walmart once said he could tell how a store was doing by count­ing the cars in its park­ing lot. What if you could do that for every store? {117-S08}
Alex quit, bought three years of im­agery from his old firm and back-tested it. When park­ing-lot traf­fic surged, the next quar­terly re­sults were good; when it fell, they were bad.

The broth­ers founded RS Metrics, RS for re­mote sens­ing, and UBS came to them to work on the Walmart data. Ajay Shah’s nephew joined later. Once, asked about pro­duc­tion at a Tesla plant, the firm flew its own plane over­head.

Then Varma pro­duced the num­ber he promised would blow minds. Two Berkeley pro­fes­sors took park­ing data from 67,000 stores and found it would have given a 4.7 per cent edge over the com­mon in­vestor. {#edge} Traders, he said, would die for 0.2 per cent.
~ It might look like fi­nance bros mak­ing a killing, Varma said. But a satel­lite pic­ture of a park­ing lot is a pic­ture of real peo­ple going in and buy­ing real things.
stories.why: An old shopkeeper’s habit be­came an in­dus­try once mea­sure­ment caught up with it. A pic­ture of a car park, Varma ar­gued, tells you how a so­ci­ety is feel­ing, be­cause the cars be­long to peo­ple spend­ing real money.
stories.postscript: Varma looked for the broth­ers on YouTube and could not find them; he promised to link them in the show notes if he did.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the Diamond brothers and Walmart’s car parks

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a scientist who bet on genes in the 1960s
stories.head: The long bet on our DNA
body: Luca Cavalli-Sforza, born around 1918, was a sci­en­tist whose deep in­ter­est was the deep past, Amit Varma said. In his day that past was read from dead things: fos­sils, ruins and early car­bon dat­ing. Scant data hard­ened into a con­ven­tional wis­dom that con­strained en­quiry.

He looked for new ways in, first through the blood groups of dif­fer­ent pop­u­la­tions. Then, in the early 1960s, he made a bet that seems in­sane now: that human his­tory would be re­vealed through our genes. {117-S01}
In the 1980s, sci­en­tists study­ing mi­to­chon­drial DNA found that we all came out of Africa. The human genome was se­quenced com­pletely for the first time in 2001. {#genome}
~ By 2009, full-genome stud­ies of the past were a full-fledged sci­ence. His vi­sion had come true.
stories.why: A sci­en­tist can bet on a kind of ev­i­dence decades be­fore the tools exist to gather it. When the ev­i­dence ar­rives, Varma said, it can show that much of what we knew was es­sen­tially wrong.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Luca Cavalli-Sforza’s wild bet

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on Peggy Mohan and the curled tongue
stories.head: Sanskrit’s mother tongue
body: Sanskrit came out of the Indo-European lan­guages, Amit Varma said, draw­ing on Peggy Mohan’s *Wanderers, Kings, Merchants*. But it is not a pure Indo-European lan­guage. {117-S03}

It has retroflex sounds, made with the tongue curled to­ward the roof of the mouth; Varma made Ajay Shah say Hindi word pairs to hear them. Persian lacks them. The Dravidian lan­guages the mi­grants met in India have them.

The rea­son was in­ti­mate. The mi­grants were mostly men, and they mar­ried local women. Children spent their first years with their moth­ers, speak­ing their lan­guage; then the boys went off to ap­pren­tice and hunt, and learned the men’s.
~ Vedic Sanskrit emerged as a blend. Later it was frozen as the lan­guage of learn­ing for a class and caste, and be­came a dead lan­guage, like Latin. Prakrit kept evolv­ing.
stories.why: Even a lan­guage held sa­cred is a blend. Languages carry the im­print of who raised the chil­dren, not just of who held power, and a lan­guage, Varma said, en­codes much else within it. {117-C05}
stories.postscript: His ex­am­ple: Tagore trans­lated from Bengali into English, some­times by Tagore him­self, does not sound that great.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Sanskrit’s retroflex sounds

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on sunlight, floating roofs and satellites
stories.head: The tank that tells tales
body: Imagine a tank of oil, Ajay Shah said. Many such tanks have a roof that sits on top of the oil, so when the tank is half empty, the roof falls to half its height.
The sun is at a known place. When the tank is com­pletely full, there is no shadow. As the oil falls, a satel­lite look­ing straight down starts to see the shadow of the sun in­side. {117-S10}
From the size of that shadow, you can es­ti­mate how full the tank is. It is, Shah said, a re­mote-sensing way to know.

~ He of­fered it as one quick story from his head, after Amit Varma’s tales of park­ing lots and iron ore, as ev­i­dence that a rev­o­lu­tion of this kind is under way. “These are amaz­ing in­no­va­tions,” he said.
stories.why: Simple ge­om­e­try and a cam­era in the sky can re­veal what sits in­side a pri­vate tank. For Shah it is one more in­stance of the cre­ative mea­sure­ment that is chang­ing what can be known.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on oil tanks and their shadows

shelf.title: Early Indians: The Story of Our Ancestors and Where We Came From
shelf.creator: Tony Joseph
shelf.why: Tony Joseph uses the genes of liv­ing peo­ple to re­con­struct thou­sands of years of Indian his­tory: the first Indians, the Harappans, the Aryan mi­gra­tion, and how caste en­dogamy set in about 2,000 years ago after mil­len­nia of in­ter­min­gling.

shelf.title: Tony Joseph on The Seen and the Unseen
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s long con­ver­sa­tion with Tony Joseph on the ge­netic his­tory of the sub­con­ti­nent, the audio com­pan­ion to Early Indians, in­clud­ing how India’s mi­grant groups mixed for thou­sands of years be­fore en­dogamy locked in.

shelf.title: Wanderers, Kings, Merchants: The Story of India through Its Languages
shelf.creator: Peggy Mohan
shelf.why: Peggy Mohan reads India’s past through its liv­ing lan­guages, doing with lan­guage what Reich and Joseph did with genes: mi­grat­ing men mar­ried local women, so chil­dren spoke their mothers’ tongue first, and Sanskrit ab­sorbed local sounds such as retroflexes.

shelf.title: Peggy Mohan on The Seen and the Unseen
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Peggy Mohan’s lin­guis­tic his­tory of India in con­ver­sa­tion, the com­pan­ion to her book Wanderers, Kings, Merchants.

shelf.title: A History of Hinduism (Ep 76 of Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Their ear­lier episode built on Manu Pillai’s ac­count of Hinduism as an as­sim­ila­tive, al­most ‘open source’ tra­di­tion.

shelf.title: Gods, Guns and Missionaries: The Making of the Modern Hindu Identity
shelf.creator: Manu Pillai
shelf.why: Manu Pillai shows how fluid Hinduism was for cen­turies and how a shared Hindu iden­tity formed grad­u­ally, first against Islam and then against the British and their mis­sion­ar­ies.

shelf.title: The Hindi Heartland
shelf.creator: Ghazala Wahab
shelf.why: Has a ‘great excerpt’ on trib­als made to tick a ‘Hindu’ box, and the mass move­ment now re­assert­ing their ear­lier iden­ti­ties.

shelf.title: Caste and the Census (Ep 417 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: A timely de­bate on what count­ing caste in the cen­sus could do to Indian so­ci­ety.

shelf.title: The Alchemy of Finance
shelf.creator: George Soros
shelf.why: Source of the con­cept that the nar­ra­tives im­posed on a sys­tem change how that sys­tem sees and shapes it­self.

shelf.title: Caste, Capitalism and Chandra Bhan Prasad (Ep 296 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: The Dalit thinker whose two he­roes are Ambedkar and Adam Smith, a pair­ing cen­tral to Amit’s hope for end­ing caste.

shelf.title: In Praise of Floods
shelf.creator: James C Scott
shelf.why: James C Scott on the di­ver­sity that ex­isted be­fore the agri­cul­tural age, and on how sup­press­ing every small dis­as­ter builds up a much big­ger one, which Amit ap­plies to bailouts and moral haz­ard.

shelf.title: Against the Grain
shelf.creator: James C Scott
shelf.why: Scott’s ac­count of how agri­cul­ture and grain-based early states made life worse for or­di­nary peo­ple, over­turn­ing the story of steady progress.

shelf.title: Stage.in
shelf.creator: Vinay Singhal
shelf.why: Vinay Singhal’s ‘Netflix for Bharat’, stream­ing con­tent in di­alects like Haryanvi and Bhojpuri: Amit’s live ex­am­ple of tech­nol­ogy and long-tail mar­kets re­vers­ing the ho­mogeni­sa­tion of di­alects.

shelf.title: The Refreshing Audacity of Vinay Singhal (Ep 291 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Entrepreneur Vinay Singhal on build­ing Stage, a di­alect-first stream­ing busi­ness that proved scep­ti­cal VCs wrong and is push­ing back against Hindi’s pres­sure on India’s di­alects, in­clud­ing a ‘re­verse mi­gra­tion from Bollywood’.

shelf.title: On the Rise of FinTechs: Credit Scoring Using Digital Footprints
shelf.creator: Tobias Berg, Valentin Burg, Ana Gombović & Manju Puri
shelf.why: Shows that dig­i­tal foot­prints pre­dict de­fault: iPhone vs Android, email provider, typos in email ad­dresses, and late-night shop­ping.

shelf.title: The Nighttime Lights of Russia (Ep 116 of Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: How satel­lite night-lights let Indian re­searchers see into the Russian econ­omy in ways tra­di­tional sta­tis­tics never could, part of the show’s se­ries on mea­sure­ment.

shelf.title: Shedding light on the Russia-Ukraine War
shelf.creator: Rounak Hande, Ayush Patnaik, Ajay Shah & Susan Thomas
shelf.why: Ajay’s co-authored paper that uses care­fully cor­rected night­time lights to read Russia’s econ­omy while of­fi­cial data is with­held: roughly flat from 2019 to 2025, with dam­age along its bor­ders and a 245 km east­ward shift in its cen­tre of mass.

shelf.title: Our Population Is Our Greatest Asset (Ep 20 of Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The ar­gu­ment that peo­ple are brains, not stom­achs: hu­mans are in­no­va­tors whose cre­ativ­ity beats scarcity, so India’s prob­lem is too few chil­dren and too lit­tle train­ing of minds, not too many peo­ple.

laughs.text: Ajay in­tro­duces ‘the great Omit Varma’ in Bengali style. Amit replies that to Ajay he’s Amit, ‘just as you are Ajay and not Ajoy. Two can play this game. Kindly con­trol.’
Amit, after Ajay’s ode to data: ‘the road to knowl­edge be­gins with data, and I would say the road to knowl­edge ends in de­spair.’

On all 7.5 bil­lion hu­mans de­scend­ing from mi­to­chon­drial Eve: ‘Why are you laugh­ing? This is a se­ri­ous sub­ject. But I sus­pect the lady would also laugh if she knew what she had wrought. All for a few mo­ments of plea­sure.’

On 3-5% Neanderthal DNA in Europeans and Asians: ‘we were hav­ing a party with Neanderthals’. So call­ing some­one a Neanderthal who ‘won’t un­der­stand art’ is re­ally an in­sult to part of our­selves.
On say­ing ‘indexes’ rather than the British ‘indices’: it’s sex­ier, ‘be­cause we don’t talk of the sises, we talk of the sexes.’
The lip­stick index failed dur­ing COVID: ‘People are wear­ing masks so they don’t need lip­stick. You un­der­stand what I’m say­ing? This is a pro­found point.’

Introducing Greenspan’s male un­der­wear index, Amit de­scribes him as an econ­o­mist who ‘loved low in­ter­est rates’. In bad times the gap be­tween un­der­wear pur­chases gets, pun not in­tended, ‘stretched’, until the elas­tic is fall­ing off com­pletely.
On the di­a­per rash index: ‘You sim­ply have to get your ba­bies all the di­a­pers they need, which is a sen­tence I never thought I’d say.’
James C Scott’s Seeing Like a State: Ajay quips its al­ter­na­tive title could be ‘State Legibility Projects Have Unintended Consequences’. He also calls cen­sus-making a Heisenberg ef­fect.
‘A lan­guage is a di­alect with an army’, the old line Amit uses to ex­plain why Bhojpuri, Maithili and Haryanvi were swal­lowed by Hindi.
Alan Greenspan’s view, per Ajay, that bet­ter mea­sure­ment yields far big­ger gains than more eco­nomic the­ory.
Hannah Arendt’s line that au­thor­i­tar­i­ans run out of peo­ple to op­press, in­voked by Ajay in the fer­til­ity dis­cus­sion.
